There is no rotation drama and no stylistic surprise here — just a goalkeeper with proven international ceiling and an iron-man club season behind him, which is broadly what a contender wants from its last line.

J. Pickford.text:
Pickford has been the model of an ever-present, dependable club keeper. He played all 38 Premier League games in both 2024 (7.26 rating across 3,420 minutes) and 2025 (7.02 across 3,432), and barely missed a session in the cups, where his marks edged higher still — 7.70 in the FA Cup in 2024, 7.50 in 2025. That is two full seasons of uninterrupted top-flight work, which matters for a 31-year-old heading into a tournament: durability and rhythm rather than a question mark over fitness or pecking order.

The slight caution is the recent trend in an England shirt. His 2026 numbers have dipped to 6.90 in two World Cup qualifiers and 6.75 in two friendlies, below his club baseline, though the samples are tiny. For a side ranked fourth in the world, none of this threatens his standing as first-choice; the club form points to a settled, reliable keeper, with the only watch being whether those modest international ratings firm up before the finals.

Y. Bounou.text:
Bounou's club work at Al-Hilal has been steady rather than spectacular: a 6.82 Pro League rating across 31 games in 2024, nudged up to 6.93 over 26 league outings in 2025. The eye-catching numbers come on the bigger stages, where he tends to raise his level — 7.42 in the 2024 AFC Champions League Elite and a tournament-best 7.78 across five FIFA Club World Cup matches in 2025. That pattern matters for a goalkeeper carrying a World Cup load, and his international form backs it up: 7.17 over seven Africa Cup of Nations games and 7.33 in three friendlies already this year.

At 34 he is an experienced, reliable last line behind a side ranked eighth by FIFA, and the data suggests a keeper who finds another gear when the games get serious. For Morocco's tournament hopes, that big-stage uplift is exactly the trait you want, even if the week-to-week league ratings read as merely solid.

M. Maignan.text:
At 30, Maignan brings the kind of metronomic club workload selectors love: 37 Serie A appearances in both 2024 and 2025, with his rating nudging up from 7.1 to 7.23 across those campaigns. The wider 2024 sample is what catches the eye — 7.22 across ten Champions League outings and a standout 7.7 in the Coppa Italia point to a goalkeeper who raised his level on bigger nights, exactly the profile France's number one needs heading into a World Cup with the top-ranked side.

The caveat sits in the international column. His club consistency hasn't always travelled: a 6.62 across five World Cup qualifiers and 6.83 in three 2026 friendlies trail the 7.33 and 7.34 he posted at the Euros and in the Nations League. That's a meaningful gap, and it leaves an open question about which version turns up in the summer. The club form says elite; the most recent France numbers say watch closely.

Alisson Becker.text:
Alisson arrives at 33 as a known quantity: a goalkeeper whose numbers have softened slightly without collapsing. His standout stretch was 2024, when he posted a 7.11 rating across 28 Premier League games and an excellent 7.62 over six Champions League outings. The 2025 club campaign reads a touch cooler — 6.78 across 26 league appearances, with the European number easing to 7.18 over six games — which fits the profile of a veteran keeper rather than a decline worth alarm.

For the tournament, the more relevant evidence is recent and international: nine World Cup qualifiers at a steady 7.18, in line with his best European work. That consistency between club and country is what matters for a Brazil side ranked sixth in the world. The friendlies dip to 6.7 is a small sample and easy to discount. On this form, Alisson remains a dependable foundation rather than a liability — neither a reason to upgrade Brazil nor one to fade them.

Diogo Costa.text:
Diogo Costa arrives at 26 as a goalkeeper trending the right way. His Porto league form ticked up from a 6.98 rating across 32 Primeira Liga appearances in 2024 to 7.07 over 33 in 2025, with his Europa League number also climbing from 6.89 to 7.05. That is not a dramatic leap, but it is steady, high-volume work — nearly 2,900 league minutes in each campaign — and the modest gain suggests a keeper settling into a consistent level rather than peaking or fading.

What matters more for a World Cup is that his international ceiling already sits above his club baseline: a 7.34 rating at the Euros and 7.23 in the Nations League. With Portugal ranked fifth in the world, the platform in front of him is strong, and a keeper who raises his game on the big stage is exactly what a deep run demands. His World Cup qualifying mark of 6.6 is the one note of caution against the optimism.

T. Courtois.text:
At 33, Courtois remains Real Madrid's first choice and a steady presence across two heavy seasons. In 2024 he posted a 7.11 league rating over 32 La Liga appearances and lifted his level in Europe, where his 7.43 across twelve Champions League games was his standout return. The 2025 campaign saw the domestic number dip slightly to 6.93 over another full 32-game, 2,880-minute league season, but the bigger stages again brought out his best: 7.47 at the FIFA Club World Cup and 7.29 in the Champions League, where he even chipped in two assists.

That consistency matters for Belgium, ranked ninth and reliant on him to keep tight games alive. His two 2026 friendly outings produced a 7.05 rating, in line with his club baseline. The pattern is clear enough — a goalkeeper who holds a solid floor over big minutes and tends to raise it in knockout football, which is exactly the profile a side outside the favourites needs in a tournament.

T. Hayakawa.text:
Tomoki Hayakawa has built his case the patient way: a full ever-present season at Kashima in the J1 League, 38 appearances and 3,420 minutes in both 2024 and 2025, with his rating climbing from 7.06 to 7.15 across those campaigns. The 2026 league season has been his strongest stretch yet — 17 games, 1,536 minutes and a 7.38 rating, the clearest sign that the 26-year-old is trending upward rather than plateauing at his peak.

The international picture is thinner and more honest. His Japan minutes have come mostly in the EAFF championship and friendlies, where the numbers cool off — a 6.64 rating across one heavier EAFF stint and just eight minutes of a friendly in 2026. That gap between consistent club form and limited senior caps is the story for a Japan side ranked 18th in the world: Hayakawa is in genuinely good touch domestically, but the tournament data suggests he profiles as a squad goalkeeper rather than a guaranteed starter.

O. Baumann.text: Oliver Baumann arrives at the tournament as a steady but unspectacular presence between the posts. His Hoffenheim seasons tell a consistent story: a 7.01 Bundesliga rating across 28 appearances in 2024, then a near-ever-present 34-game campaign in 2025 at a slightly lower 6.81. That's a goalkeeper trusted with the bulk of his club's minutes for two straight seasons — durable, dependable, rarely the difference-maker. The concern is direction of travel. At 35, his most recent form for Germany dips below those club numbers, with three 2026 friendlies returning just a 6.27 rating, softer than the 6.92 he managed across six World Cup qualifiers. For a side ranked tenth, that's a thin margin to lean on. Baumann's record suggests a safe pair of hands who keeps the floor reasonably high rather than a shot-stopper who steals knockout ties. The friendly dip is a small sample, but it nudges the questions about whether he can lift his level when Germany need a save that matters.

So treat the winner as well-signposted but not sealed, and the total as a genuinely open question rather than the formality the market implies.

review.text:

It was a clean continuation of the home side's recent form, and the scoreline landed exactly on the model's single most likely outcome: 2-0 sat top of the projected scores at 15.4 percent, just ahead of 1-0. A 2.06 expected-goals figure for Mexico against 0.56 for South Africa described this game well in advance, and the shutout chimed with a below-even both-teams-to-score read of 38 percent.

This was a good night for both the model and the market, with little to separate them. The model priced Mexico at 72.2 percent to win; Polymarket had them at 69.5 cents — close agreement that South Africa, ranked 60th to Mexico's 15th, would struggle to find a foothold. The locked bracket pick of 1-0 Mexico nailed the result if not the exact margin, and a first-to-score read of 72.5 percent for the hosts captured how the game was always likely to flow. A straightforward call, and a correct one.

The model's numbers say this is a contest the Czechs can win or draw, and the market's all-or-nothing pricing leaves no room for that.

review.text:
South Korea opened their Group A campaign with a 2-1 win over the Czech Republic in Guadalajara, turning a tight contest into the kind of narrow home victory the numbers leaned toward without ever promising. The Czechs, the more valuable squad on paper at €188m to Korea's €139m and unbeaten in their previous nine before kickoff, got on the scoresheet but couldn't take a point from the Estadio Akron.

Grade this one a clean hit for the model. It made South Korea favorites at 47.4% to win, with the draw at 27.7% and the Czechs trailing on 24.9%, and the result landed squarely on the right side. The exact 2-1 scoreline was the fifth-likeliest line at 9.1%, and with an xG read of 1.46 to 0.98 the model expected Korea to edge the goal count without a blowout — which is exactly what happened. BTTS came in too, just ahead of the model's near-coin-flip 48.6%. Our locked bracket pick, a 1-1 that called the home result correctly, also graded as a hit. A solid, unflashy night for the projections.

The numbers had painted Canada as overwhelming favourites at home: a 76.97% win probability, an expected goals edge of 2.36 to 0.57, and a three-in-four chance of scoring first. Instead Bosnia, who arrived unbeaten across their last six qualifiers, found the goal that turned a projected rout into a point apiece. The draw was priced at just 16.11%, and both teams scoring was rated only 39.93%, so the way this game played out sat firmly in the model's blind spot.

That makes for an honest miss to grade. The locked bracket pick was 2-0 Canada, the single most likely scoreline at 14.81%, and it landed nowhere near — the actual 1-1 ranked only fifth on the model's board at 7.58%. The market echoed the same heavy lean toward the hosts, so neither view comes out of this looking good. Bosnia's recent form, including draws with Italy and Austria, perhaps deserved more respect than a 6.92% away price allowed. A clear reminder that 77% is not 100%.

review.text:

review.text:

review.text:
